/.title: Which occupations' work goes to AI next (Anthropic Economic Index)
/.company: Claude.ai conversations classified by occupation in the Anthropic Economic Index
/.problem: Can we predict each occupation group's share of AI conversations in the next Economic Index release?
/.protocol_line: Every prediction is made from earlier releases only and scored on the next release; the design was frozen on the first two cutoffs.
/.situation: Anthropic publishes the share of Claude.ai conversations that perform each O*NET task, release by release since February 2025. Computer and mathematical work led from the start; education, arts and media, office and sales work have taken larger shares since.
/.data_used: Six Anthropic Economic Index releases from February 2025 to June 2026 (Hugging Face Anthropic/EconomicIndex at a pinned revision; data CC BY, card metadata MIT): the global share of Claude.ai conversations by O*NET task, mapped to the 22 SOC major occupation groups.
/.intro: Rebuilds Claude.ai use as 22 occupation groups, each a population of simulated workers whose use of the assistant follows a diffusion path; each group's share of conversations is its use relative to every other group's. From each release the simulation predicts every group's share in the next release, and is scored against what the next release reported. The alternative asks how the mix would shift if office and administrative workers took up the assistant twice as fast.
/.world: The 22 SOC major occupation groups, each a population of 1,000 simulated workers; the groups' shares of conversations are rescaled to sum to 100% at every release.
/.source: manifests/sources.json (Anthropic Economic Index, Hugging Face Anthropic/EconomicIndex, pinned revision)

evaluation.cutoffs: 4 cutoffs: the releases of 2025-09-15, 2026-01-15, 2026-03-24 and 2026-06-26, each predicted from the releases before it
evaluation.calibration: at each cutoff, backtests on earlier releases

scenarios.title: AI use by occupation as it happened: every group carried forward to the next release
scenarios.description: From each release, carry every occupation group's simulated workers forward to the next release: workers start or stop using the assistant with the hazards of the diffusion path calibrated on the earlier releases, and each group's share of conversations is its use relative to all groups.

scenarios.title: What if office and administrative workers had taken up the assistant twice as fast?
scenarios.summary: Office and administrative support workers who do not use the assistant start at twice the simulated hazard; same cutoffs and seeds.
scenarios.description: An enterprise roll-out aimed at office and administrative support work doubles the probability that a non-using worker in that group starts using the assistant in each period. Every other group behaves as in the simulation of what happened; shares are rescaled to sum to 100%. The size of the change is authored, not estimated.

takeaways: On 2 held-out cutoffs (44 predictions) the simulation's error was 0.86 pp, equal to the best standard method (no change, 0.86 pp): 0.0% less error.
Accuracy, 100 x (1 - error / mean actual): 81.2% for the simulation and 81.2% for no change.

The next release: 0.86 pp for the simulation, 0.86 pp for no change; 82% of actual outcomes inside the simulation's 90% range.

takeaways: On 2 held-out cutoffs (44 predictions) the simulation's error was 0.86 pp, equal to the best standard method (no change, 0.86 pp): 0.0% less error.
Accuracy, 100 x (1 - error / mean actual): 81.2% for the simulation and 81.2% for no change.

The next release: 0.86 pp for the simulation, 0.86 pp for no change; 82% of actual outcomes inside the simulation's 90% range.

sections.heading: What was predicted
sections.body: Rebuilds Claude.ai use as 22 occupation groups, each a population of simulated workers whose use of the assistant follows a diffusion path; each group's share of conversations is its use relative to every other group's. From each release the simulation predicts every group's share in the next release, and is scored against what the next release reported. The alternative asks how the mix would shift if office and administrative workers took up the assistant twice as fast.

/scenarios.card_summary: Carry the occupation mix forward to the next release.

/scenarios.title: What if office and administrative workers had taken up the assistant twice as fast?
/scenarios.summary: Office and administrative support workers who do not use the assistant start at twice the simulated hazard; same cutoffs and seeds.
/scenarios.description: An enterprise roll-out aimed at office and administrative support work doubles the probability that a non-using worker in that group starts using the assistant in each period. Every other group behaves as in the simulation of what happened; shares are rescaled to sum to 100%. The size of the change is authored, not estimated.
/scenarios.card_summary: Double assumed uptake in office and administrative work.

properties.description: The company or group being simulated. Root of the org-unit tree.
A division, department or team. Units nest (part_of) and hold people and roles.
An employee, played as a digital twin: real covariates, a fixed trait layer, weekly latent states and a seat whose policy makes its decisions. Archetypes when the data has no individuals.
A job in this organisation (e.g. purchasing clerk, software engineer). Bound to one O*NET-SOC occupation; performs the instance's activities.
An O*NET-SOC 31.0 occupation, the shared vocabulary that lets roles in different companies be compared.
O*NET generalized work activity: the top level of the activity hierarchy (41 items).
O*NET intermediate work activity (332 items), between GWAs and DWAs.
O*NET detailed work activity (2,087 items). Every instance activity maps to at least one DWA.
An O*NET occupation-specific task statement.
Something a role does in this organisation on the simulated clock (an event-log step, a customer call, a code review). Carries a weight and a remote-feasibility flag.
The unit of work that flows through activities: a purchase-order line, a case, a ticket.
A document or output an activity produces (invoice, merged code change, review).
A tool or software system (ERP, CRM, code repository) that exposes capabilities.
One thing a system can do, in the MCP sense; activities use capabilities. Automating a capability is a policy lever.
A place work happens: an office, a home, a plant. Hybrid-work policies move people between locations.
A vendor, client or customer outside the organisation that interacts with its activities.
A communication between people (email, chat, meeting invitation).
An intervention or scenario lever: a work-from-home offer, an automation, a hiring wave. Affects roles, activities, capabilities, units or locations.
One recorded occurrence on the clock: a person performed an activity on a work item at a time. The trace is a sequence of events.
A latent, time-varying quantity attached to a person: job satisfaction, work-life balance, attachment, commute burden. Updated weekly by the kernel.
